Their findings revealed that these systems can be represented as critical lattice models derived from random log-gases. These same systems can also be interpreted as moderate deviations from the Gaussian free field, resulting in numerous SLE processes being driven by them. Here, we demonstrate that these systems can be coupled with the Gaussian free field on planar domains. These couplings have a number of equivalent formulations: (1) given an arbitrary realization of the driving process of the log-gas, we can construct a associated Gaussian free field and SLE boundary conditions; (2) these couplings are unique up to a dependence on the realization of the driving process of the log-gas; (3) these couplings can be extended to include rank-dependent factors; (4) these couplings can be represented through the relationship between the rank of the driving process of the log-gas and the rank of the rank-one perturbation in the Gaussian free field.

This research focuses on establishing the unconditional stability of the Navier-Stokes equations for periodic initial conditions under a fixed force influence, with the key criterion being the $L_\infty$-norm of the solution's real part. Unlike existing stability assessments, which often rely on the $L_2$-norm, this study derives a priori estimates directly within the $L_\infty$-space. To achieve this novel result, the paper utilizes the Fourier expansion of the solution in contrast to earlier works that employed Leray-Schauder theory and the Fourier expansion in $L_2$-space.

We've developed a verification method for quantum computation that doesn't rely on the assumption that quantum computers are reliable. Our approach uses a straightforward and efficient method to create a detailed description of a computation's process, which can be easily compared with the expected outcome. Specifically, we've designed a protocol that allows a quantum computer to confidently declare the results of its calculations, even in scenarios with high error rates and limited reliance on randomness. Our method is based on a precise description of the quantum measurement process and utilizes a detailed analysis of the properties of symmetric quantum measurements.

Recent breakthroughs in neural radiance fields have enabled implicit 3D object
rendering with high accuracy, but its application in biology is largely unexplored.
We employ neural radiance fields to model cell shapes implicitly by learning
point-wise density and position values, achieving compact and detailed
representations of cell shapes. Our approach innovates by introducing a new
point sampling method tailored to mitigate the instability when sampling points
arbitrarily in the implicit space. We also propose a new-accurate evaluation
metric tailored to cell modeling. Experimental results demonstrate that our
method surpasses existing LiDAR-based methods in predicting cell shapes from
microscopic images, and even generalizes effectively to unseen cell types.

Reinforcement learning techniques have yielded significant advancements in artificial intelligence, yielding understandable representations of geographic data. These representations have a clear structure - a state space that models real-world environments and an action space that simulates agent movement. Given sufficient training, artificial agents can learn efficient navigation strategies through agent-based representations. Despite the structural similarities, these models lack a direct connection to real-world geography, differing from human perceptions of space. This study examines whether reinforcement learning can be employed to generate biologically plausible geographic models that capture agents' movements in relation to their surroundings. Our novel approach utilizes an encoder network to consolidate nearby locations into a single state, providing a unified view of the environment. Additionally, we propose a novel metric called proximity variance, measuring the dispersion of locations within a state, thus quantifying spatial structure. Our results indicate that these models can learn efficient navigation strategies on various geographic datasets, including real-world driving scenarios and synthetic worlds with distinct structures. These findings support the use of reinforcement learning to develop geographic models that mimic biological processes, as evidenced by the structural properties of these representations.

Recent research on quantum dynamics across various systems has discovered a specific type of non-stationary Markov chain known as 'hard-drive' dipoles, characterized by stationary probabilities that can be expressed as high-degree rational numbers, as opposed to the typical transcendental values. This unique form of dipole offers potential benefits in terms of computational efficiency and storage requirements. A key challenge lies in developing theoretical models that can accommodate these non-retrograde Markov chains, facilitating the creation of a broader class of non-stationary bound states known as 'hard-drive' states, which can be achieved through the integration of stationary states and the temporal reversal of system components.

The challenge of sound event localization and detection involves pinpointing the presence of multiple overlapping sound sources in an audio recording. Current solutions, primarily based on Deep Neural Networks, face difficulties in detecting faint sources amidst loud ones and those that are similar in sound. To improve performance under these conditions, this research proposes an enhanced method that leverages filter orientation in a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN). By achieving a precise spatial representation of sound source direction through channel rotation, this method surpasses state-of-the-art results in the SESCHD dataset evaluation. Additionally, a novel architecture using rectangular filters outperforms a comparable CNN-based approach.

Concurrent transmission based wireless systems, allowing multiple users to share the same frequency, take advantage of the inherent properties of superposition transmission to increase spectral efficiency and user experience. This text explores the advancements in such systems, starting with NT-based (multi-user) transmission methods like Gaussian mixture and Gaussian-Variate, which improve performance in complex scenarios. It also delves into more sophisticated approaches, such as deep learning powered models, to optimize applications like visible light communication, and discusses performance evaluation methods for these complex systems. Further research is suggested in areas like AI-enabled transmission methods and experimental demonstrations of these novel techniques.

The majority of signal examination techniques focus on either the underlying signal or its individual components, overlooking the inherent spatial relationships present in spectrogram level contours. By applying stochastic geometry to these contours, this study develops novel methods to assess spatial consistency, density, and correlation within the spectrogram, providing a comprehensive approach to analyzing spatial relationships. These methods are further combined with intensity analysis, where relevant parameters are adjusted to create a stochastic geometry spectrum analysis (SGSA) framework that surpasses traditional spectrum analysis. To verify the efficacy of the proposed approach, the study compares its performance to established signal examination techniques on a range of synthetic and real-world signal scenarios.

We've developed a practical method for identifying multiple clusters of synchronized neural populations in large networks of interacting spiking neurons through an unsupervised approach. This novel technique dynamically creates and updates groups based on the connections between neurons, effectively detecting different types of synchronized patterns within the network. Unlike other methods, this approach doesn't prefer larger clusters over smaller ones, making it ideal for detecting diverse regimes including multiple stable patterns of chimera states. Additionally, by analyzing the quantities formed within these groups, we've observed a scaling pattern in the numbers of clusters and synchronized populations as the network size increases, which transitions at critical thresholds related to the network's local connectivity.

Our research introduces a random force module designed for N-body simulations, which we've successfully integrated into the REBOUND software framework. This module mimics real planetary systems by applying noise to these systems, helping scientists study the effects of external influences and the long-term behavior of these systems. The random force module supports multiple types of noise, including Gaussian, exponential, and power law variations, and can be used to model a variety of scenarios, such as the long-term stability of planetary systems and the characteristics of circumplanetary disks.

We have developed a comprehensive approach to continuous feedback control in quantum systems using the quantum Fokker-Planck equation. Our method employs the quantum conditional Fokker-Planck equation to analyze the dynamics of quantum systems influenced by random driving forces and deliberate feedback adjustments. By integrating the quantum Fokker-Planck equation with the It\^o formula, we've derived a general solution to the quantum feedback control problem, providing a framework for optimizing system performance. The results of our theory are applicable to a broad range of systems, including open quantum systems, as demonstrated by specific examples involving two-level systems and its practical implications for quantum information processing.

We examine two-dimensional disk packing patterns that get clogged when placed in channels of varying widths. Both static and dynamic packing methods yield alternating sequences of disk placement. In the static case, a grid pattern emerges, whereas in the dynamic case, a Hales-Macaulay-like pattern is produced, similar to those observed in three-dimensional packings.

Research into ENSO's impact on global climate phenomena using multiplicity approaches often faces two primary challenges: accurately categorizing ENSO types and quantifying their distinct spatial patterns. This study addresses these concerns by employing cluster analysis to categorize ENSO events based on spatial patterns in the Pacific, using a model that incorporates both remote drivers and ENSO fluctuations. Their findings reveal that the traditional concept of ENSO types needs revision. This research focuses on the distinct ways different ENSO types affect global precipitation patterns, particularly on very low and elevated seasonal precipitation. Their analysis shows that each ENSO type has a unique signature in precipitation patterns, indicating the varying influences of ENSO phases on global precipitation regimes.

Supermassive black holes at the hearts of galaxies emerge from smaller seed black holes through a process that has been poorly understood. Researchers have proposed multiple theories, including one that massive black holes originated from nearby massive star clusters that dispersed following a galaxy collision. Using data from the Hubble telescope, a massive black hole in the dwarf galaxy Leo I was found to be surrounded by a unique ring-like structure consisting of gas and stars. This finding supports a long-abandoned theory that massive black holes can be born directly in dwarf galaxies. To validate this observation, a model was developed to simulate the collision and its effects on the galaxy, and the results revealed a similar ring-like structure around a black hole. This structure could provide crucial insights into the early history of a galaxy's black hole formation.

In systems with electronic flat bands, quantum properties such as correlation, topological characteristics and interference can be inherently present. We have investigated the flat band effect on magnetoresistance in the three-dimensional kagome metal system, which is known for exhibiting multifarious ferromagnetic ground states and flat bands. By employing a time-reversal symmetry breaking approach using an in-plane magnetic field, we have observed adverse magnetoresistance (lower resistance in the non-magnetized state) in the very close proximity to the flat band region. Our experimental and computational studies indicate that this peculiar behavior results from the flat band's enhanced correlation and geometric effects. This unique response provides further evidence of the flat band's presence in the kagome metal and the intricate interplay between its band structure and magnetic properties.

The integration of public genomics and transcriptomics data allows for an examination of how transcript variations relate to observable traits in humans. By combining datasets from multiple sources, researchers can identify variations in human genes and their association with distinct phenotypes. Utilizing a comprehensive approach to analyze data from the HapMap3 project and the GTEx dataset, researchers have discovered novel genetic modifications linked to various human characteristics. Notably, investigations into 18 human characteristics, including body composition and lymph node presence, uncovered hundreds of significant associations between genomic locations and these phenotypes. These findings highlight the significance of transcriptomic data in understanding the underlying mechanisms of human gene function and provide a foundation for further research into the genomics and phenomics of human genes.

Recent research by Pendavingh and Van Strien identified examples of infinite arrangements of lines on a 2-sphere, with spherical symmetry groups that permit transitive actions on flags. These examples served as counterpoints to earlier findings by Wolfart. This study aims to expand upon these examples by reducing the requirements for the spherical symmetry groups, lowering the index from 3 to 2. As a result, the examples provided here diminish a previous conjecture regarding the minimal spherical symmetry groups, as proposed by Wolfart, where he speculated that spherical symmetry groups with transitive flag actions could have orders not exceeding 29.

To analyze the influence of Coulomb interaction on the temporal behavior of entropy in a two-electron impurity atom, we employ the time-dependent density functional theory with the constrained density functional theory. We measure entropy utilizing micro-entropies linked to $Q$-distributions, namely, von Neumann and Fisher information entropies. We examine under what conditions the time-dependent Hamiltonian is quadratic and evaluate the impact of Coulomb interaction on entropic behavior and its relationship with inter-electron correlation. We further investigate variational bounds on the time-dependent Fisher information entropy within the framework of spin-free statistics. Our results demonstrate that entropy behavior mirrors that of the system's ground state, exhibiting exponential decay without Coulomb interaction and slower decay with increasing Coulomb interaction. We relate this to the correlation between electrons, establishing that this correlation limits the decay rate of entropy. We also show that the Fisher information entropy decays faster than von Neumann entropy, with their difference exhibiting an inverse power-law behavior. We attribute this to electron pairing in the system, enabling a deeper understanding of entropy behavior and its connection to electron correlation.

We provide a thorough examination of the concept of extensive binary systems in the framework of Ashtekar's variables, incorporating the generation of configuration space metrics. Our analysis directly addresses the prevailing controversy surrounding the binary system's gravity test, showcasing that the line element's metric is indeed a non-trivial solution to Einstein's equations when the mass density of the line is considered in a 3D space. Additionally, our study reveals that this metric is invariant under certain group actions, and we speculate that this property may be significant in future research on loop quantum gravity.

In the context of multiplicative linear logic, specific connectives serve to control the structural features of proof terms, analogous to cut elimination in sequent calculus. This work expands on this concept by incorporating cut-elimination within a denotational framework that incorporates proof nets. Proof nets facilitate an efficient representation of proof terms, allowing for the implementation of a proof-reduction system that mirrors the reduction of the underlying language in which they are embedded. This system's efficacy is demonstrated through a proof of soundness and a derivation-free representation of the original denotational model.

One major issue in forecasting financial markets is the challenge of timing, accurately predicting when to enter a market that will harmonize with other investments. This study proposes an original approach to forecast the likelihood and duration of synchronization among financial time series using cross-correlation analysis of their patterns of temporal connection. By applying this novel method to high-frequency financial data, we demonstrate its effectiveness in predicting the conditions of synchronization, outperforming established techniques and paving the way for improved timing strategies in financial investments.

By incorporating the inertia of electrons and holes, we have derived equations of motion that include Dicke-like and Rabi-like interactions, which are capable of generating correlated electron-phonon and spin-vibration states through coherent coupling. These equations reveal that both electron- and hole-phonon interactions possess the same dynamic character, while the energy exchange between electrons and phonons is facilitated through the absorption or emission of phonons by electrons. Additionally, we have demonstrated that strong e-ph interactions can lead to the stabilization of negative U states in doped semiconductors and the creation of multiquantum entangled e-ph states. Finally, we have analyzed the possibility of observing entangled e-ph states via microwave spectroscopy in silicon.

Predicting click-through rates (CTR) for advertisements is a complex challenge, especially when dealing with ads that contain little text. Research has demonstrated that incorporating ad visuals can improve CTR prediction accuracy, yet most existing methods overlook this aspect. To address this gap, our paper proposes EmergeNet, a model that uses visuals from ads to enhance CTR prediction for new ads. Specifically, EmergeNet leverages the ad's visual elements to generate an embedding that is then integrated with traditional ad features. This approach has been extensively validated through experiments on real-world data, which revealed a significant 3.5% improvement in CTR prediction accuracy across various metrics. Notably, the results also showed that EmergeNet can effectively learn to compensate for incomplete ad content by incorporating visuals, thus delivering better performance than models that solely rely on text features.

Business process management systems rely heavily on business process models to simulate, analyze and implement business processes. Business process models can be represented as business process models (BPMN), organization modeling languages (ODM) or enterprise architecture frameworks. Business process models are used to identify limitations in business processes, which can be addressed through business process optimization. The BPMN language supports the representation of business processes but lacks the ability to model certain limitations, prompting the need for additional constraints such as limits on output, forward, and loop cardinalities. The BPMN constraints are insufficient to express all business process limitations, which can be represented using the OD M language with additional limitations. This document presents the BPMN Editor Tool (BPMN Editor) that enables business process analysts to identify and address process issues by identifying process limitations, which can be optimized through process optimization. The BPMN Editor Tool represents business process models as BPMN, OD M with additional limitations, or enterprise architecture frameworks to address process issues. The BPMN Editor Tool supports the identification, analysis, and optimization of business process limitations, which can be temporarily disabled or addressed to improve the business process. The BPMN Editor Tool also enables business process analysts to identify process issues that cannot be resolved through process optimization, which can be addressed by process re-engineering. The BPMN Editor Tool is presented as a technical document with installation, configuration, and usage instructions, as well as a user guide and source code. The BPMN Editor Tool is

Quantifying wildfire impacts on the global atmosphere has become increasingly crucial due to their expanding reach and effects on air quality and public health. However, inferring wildfire aerosols from satellite imagery is clouded by obscuring aerosol-driven clouds, necessitating novel methods. We've developed a physics-based probabilistic framework to estimate wildfire aerosol density by leveraging multiple satellite images and forecasting models. This approach incorporates nonlinear filter processes and an advection-diffusion equation, informed by random fluctuations. To account for the variability in aerosol clouds, we applied the Eulerian method, resulting in a physics-based statistical model. This method was validated on a dataset containing wildfire-induced aerosol data and forecasting models, and outperformed comparison methods in predicting wildfire aerosol density.

Recent research has revealed how smartphone data can be exploited by advertisers, 
who are subject to strict data regulations. To protect users' location privacy, 
existing methods typically assume that collected data is entirely anonymous and 
fail to account for potential prior knowledge that might be held by advertisers. 
This work builds on prior research by Eisenberger et al. and proposes an enhanced 
location tracking scheme that takes into consideration specific conditional 
circumstances in which location data is collected, thereby providing a more 
realistic and protected location tracking service for users.

Data analysis of resting-state fMRI has a unique hurdle in balancing signal reliability with high spatial resolution to cover the entire brain. We investigated how different approaches affect results by analyzing a large dataset of multiscale connectivity data. By examining the relationship between spatial resolution and reliability, we identified a sweet spot for optimal results and confirmed through simulations that high spatial resolution leads to inaccurate conclusions on small scales. We further demonstrated that multi-resolution analysis offers more accurate information than single high-resolution imaging, and showcased its potential by improving accuracy in mood disorder prediction based on connectivity data.

Building on Wylie and Hendrickson's work on directed networks, we explored the convergence of the Wylie-Hendrickson equation to Fourier's heat equation as the network's density approaches infinity, under the condition that the directed network satisfies a lower Ricci curvature constraint known as $\kappa_\ast$. We also established that the Wylie-Hendrickson equation leads to an over-smoothing effect near high-density nodes, and that this phenomenon is magnified at extremely high densities, resulting in infinite heat flux and concentration of measure near the highest-density nodes. Notably, our findings indicate that the outer boundary of the heat dissipation area grows quadratically with increasing time, and that the inner concentration phenomenon is intensified at even higher densities, resulting in a complete inner concentration of measure.

Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention due to the vast user base of social media and text messaging in India. Leveraging the effectiveness of pre-trained models in various NLP tasks, researchers have developed pre-trained models tailored to process code-mixed texts. Nonetheless, enhancing the pre-trained model alone is insufficient to achieve optimal results; proposers often employ fixed positional encoding to capture position-dependent information. This approach, while efficient, comes with drawbacks; it fails to differentiate between similar positions or incorporates position-related information that may not be relevant. To address these limitations, this paper introduces PESTO (Transition Point based Dynamic and Relative Positional Encoding), a novel positional encoding method. PESTO employs a transition point encoder to distinguish between different positions and a dynamic encoder that amplifies position-related characteristics. To validate the efficacy of the proposed model, the researchers designed and implemented a new dynamic positional encoding task. Experimental findings on the Hindi-English code-mixed dataset from the TREC data release demonstrate the superiority of the PESTO model over the existing pre-trained models and a position encoding method. Moreover, the researchers analyzed the results of ablation studies and manual position encoding to assess the impact of various positional encoding components and position encoding techniques. The empirical outcomes confirm that PESTO outperforms the current position encoding methods and surpasses the performance of the leading models.

Using a cluster extension of the fixed-nuclei density functional theory, we calculate the phonon spectra of three different H$_{2}$S and H$_{2}$O molecules at various pressures, focusing on how molecular vibrations affect the superconducting properties of H$_{3}$S under high pressure. By considering the influence of molecular vibrations within and outside the Fermi surface, we find that their dispersion patterns can either amplify or diminish the doping effect caused by pressure, depending on their wave vectors. When these molecular vibrations reach the critical point where their curvature changes drastically, their impact on superconducting critical temperature reaches a significant peak. Based on this understanding, we propose that the critical temperature of H$_{3}$S can be described by both pressure and a specific point where its underpressure structure matches that of high-temperature superconductors, leading to a turning-point-like behavior in the T$_{c}$-P phase diagram.

Fisher's fundamental theorem in evolutionary biology connects the rate of population fitness increase with the average effect of newly mutated genes at a specific time. This study demonstrates that both aspects of this theorem are accurate and based on a straightforward mathematical principle, which also justifies the widespread statistical analysis of population data and the widespread reliance of researchers on the concept of heritability. Furthermore, this theorem's credibility has significant implications for a wide range of related population studies, including those involving quantitative genetics and neutral theory models.

This paper presents a novel approach to improving the mobility and resilience of a bipedal robot using propellant-assisted locomotion, with the goal of overcoming rough terrain and high-gravity challenges. Building on the principles of dynamic walking, we've developed an integrated model that simultaneously controls bipedal gait and propellant pulse, leveraging a meta-heuristic to optimize step-to-step behavior. Through simulations and testing on a 1G gravity table, we've demonstrated that this hybrid control system allows the robot to achieve successful and robust dynamics on difficult terrain, even in high-gravity environments.

This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel maps to boost monocular or stereo vision system relocalization capabilities. A distinct approach is utilized to generate compact, actionable 3D maps that remain consistent across changing environments, unaffected by internal camera variations. By focusing on surfel-based 3D mapping, our method generates local maps as needed, both for localization and mapping processes, thereby reducing storage and computation requirements. Furthermore, we integrate existing methods for both 3D map-assisted localization and continuous time-based localization to create a hybrid system that combines the benefits of both approaches. To mitigate the issue of the complexity of learning-based features in visual relocalization, we employ a feature learning network that generates robust, position-agnostic features from low-resolution image tiles. Moreover, we optimize the fusion of map and camera information to resist potential chain failures. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art techniques using only 3D map-based visual relocalization. Additionally, our method also exhibits superior performance in scenarios involving significant position and orientation changes.

Federated Learning is a pioneering technique for decentralized model training that successfully balances data privacy and accuracy. Recently, researchers combined it with Semi-Supervised Learning methods, leading to novel, customized FL schemes, like FedSSL, which can effectively utilize clients' unlabeled data. These approaches, however, overlook a critical issue, causing non-deterministic model convergence and confusing results. This paper addresses this problem by investigating the inherent challenges in customized FL schemes and proposing Ambiguity Reduction for Customized FL (ARCFL), a framework that clarifies the ambiguity and guarantees model convergence. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of ARCFL in improving customized FL schemes.

Simulations of second-long colliding systems comprising black holes and neutrons stars have been conducted in a new study. These collisions result in the displacement of merger products, central disk formation, and powerful jet emissions similar to those observed in active galactic nuclei. The intensity of initial magnetic fields in these simulations was examined, leading to the discovery of magnetohydrodynamic dynamics in the disk and jet formation. Variations in initial magnetic field orientation and intensity led to notable differences in disk mass and jet power. The study also utilized diverse equations of stellar stability to gain insight into how colliding binaries would influence running out of pressure support in compact stars. Differences based on the complexity of stellar stability were discovered in disk mass, jet power, and the total mass and distribution of merger products. The intense radiation produced in these collisions was also simulated, showing how collisions involving more stable stars and higher magnetic field strengths result in brighter emissions.

A distorted invariant of a closed Riemann surface has been developed, which is tied to the volume of a specific distorted metric. It possesses properties of additivity and semi-positiveness, similar to the Chern-Simons invariant. It also exhibits behavior akin to a degree, as it remains unchanged under certain types of distortions. It has been shown that its distortion invariant is equivalent to the Chern-Simons invariant on surfaces with trivial tangent bundles that exhibit trivial distorting characteristics. Furthermore, calculations for simple examples have been undertaken.

This paper examines the convergence of a class of Q-processes based on a Galton-Watson process, showing that under specific conditions, such processes converge uniformly to a random change of measure. We also investigate the asymptotic behavior of Q-processes driven by random walk and branching processes, finding different types of convergence in varying circumstances. Furthermore, the study explores the consistent convergence of Q-processes, demonstrating that these processes can converge to a mixture of different distributions under certain conditions.

The graphene surface plasmon resonance produces an extremely strong and localized electric field when excited at terahertz frequencies. We have developed a novel technique to measure the force exerted by this field on a single nanoparticle. The outcome reveals a remarkable capacity for the nanoparticle to move with speeds exceeding 10,000 times the speed of a typical optical trap. The extraordinary mobility is attributed to the unique property of graphene to create a gapless and extremely strong electric field between the nanoparticle and the graphene surface. This finding holds potential for innovative applications in the fields of material science and optomechanics.

In the fast-paced environment of an emergency department (ED), timing is crucial when it comes to intervening with patients who are experiencing a decline in their flow of work (FW). The impact of intervention duration - the time spent helping a patient - on patient outcomes varies greatly depending on individual circumstances and is often influenced by the patient's level of need. To optimize interventions and minimize delays in the ED, it is essential to identify a typical intervention duration that balances patient care with operational efficiency. To achieve this, researchers employed a multivariate typical value approach, using data from over 14,000 patient visits and objective measures of patient need and outcomes. The analysis revealed a typical intervention duration of around 20 minutes in the ED setting. Notably, the most representative intervention durations varied between 16 and 28 minutes based on different definitions of typicality. The research provides insight into how intervention durations differ and are defined, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of the complex operational dynamics at play in the emergency department.

A persistent problem in long-term autonomous collaboration involves establishing a framework where multiple agents can demonstrate local stability through predictable behavior, even in the presence of frequent temporary disruptions. We address this challenge by examining the stability of a simple multi-agent system where each agent follows a straightforward rule, negotiated through a communicative and computational effort among the agents. Through both theoretical and experimental analyses, we establish that this system can maintain local stability under a specific range of parameters and demonstrate its practical applicability in a robotic network.

The ALICE experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has investigated correlations between the polarization of particles and the charge of particles in Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. The experiment analyzed the angular connections of same-sign particle pairs born from the same initial collisions and found that these connections were influenced by the collision's direction and number of charges. The influence of the Chiral Magnetic Effect was then limited by reanalyzing data that took into account a new method of connection representation, resulting in a significant reduction of the influence in central collisions and an agreement with a model that predicts influence based on collision properties.

The surge in online crowdfunding has prompted a pressing need to address the issue of trust and security in transaction processes, as well as understanding the behavior and decision-making processes of the crowdfunding crowd. This study concentrated on analyzing the characteristics associated with successful online fundraising events in two specific platforms, Crowdfunder UK and Indiegogo. The research involved extracting relevant features from transaction data, the completion rate of fundraising goals, and the impact of various influencer factors, followed by a comparative analysis of the importance of these features in predicting successful fund-raising events on both platforms. The results showed a high level of agreement among the machine learning models in identifying the key features associated with successful fund-raising events, with the top three factors including the fundraising goal, event description, and influencer activity, as prioritized by the experts. The research further highlighted potential avenues for improving the security and trust in transaction processes on crowdfunding platforms, as well as modifying the feature extraction approach to better match the specific requirements of each platform.

As cyber threats evolve, organizations face an increasingly difficult decision about how to prioritize their cybersecurity investments. A potential solution lies in a collaborative cyber hazard intelligence sharing system, allowing them to gather valuable insights while maintaining data sovereignty. Yet, a major obstacle stands in the way - the trust issue. A proposed framework aims to overcome this challenge by leveraging a blind PL federated learning framework, allowing multiple organizations to co-train a collaborative model without revealing their individual data. The resulting model can be deployed on each organization's system, enabling them to classify incoming network traffic without sharing their data. A practical demonstration of this approach, showing promising results and outperforming existing methods.

A key challenge in utilizing humanoid robots effectively lies in efficiently sequencing their numerous joints and limbs to mimic human hand movements, making seamless interaction with everyday objects possible. The majority of existing approaches frame this task as a traditional routing problem and apply solution-ranking techniques, evaluating hand poses through metrics such as path length or time, with little consideration for the underlying joint and limb movement mechanics. In contrast, we introduce the concept of clustering-oriented routing, which acknowledges the complexities of robot limbs and develops a greedy algorithm to produce high-quality sequences. Our approach is complemented by a method for creating meaningful clusters based on shared objectives, resulting in robust and generalizable performance, as evidenced by both simulation results and in-lab experiments involving a real iRobotino humanoid.

This study accelerates the development of LDMOS by incorporating a novel structure, the SiMOSFET. A 300mm CMOS process was modified to incorporate three different SiMOSFET designs. The primary goal was to increase the device's agility, defined as the ratio of transconductance to resistance, a crucial factor for high-frequency power amplifier design. Measurements revealed that the designed SiMOSFETs surpassed the performance of conventional LDMOS devices, achieving enhanced agility levels. Furthermore, the devices demonstrated robustness and consistent results across different measurements.

In any team setting, member coordination is measured by Synchrony, a factor that can be enhanced by regular in-group interactions, but deteriorates when individual members have differing opinions on critical issues. A new model has been developed to quantify Synchrony in dynamic systems with diverse theories applicable, including theories of stability and consensus. This model reveals a link between team performance and team dynamics, particularly how differences within a team can affect its performance when interacting with an external dynamic system. For instance, when a team is tasked with controlling the level of a complex substance, their inability to agree on the appropriate action can lead to disastrous consequences, even if each individual has a correct understanding of the system's dynamics.

A growing issue in AI systems is origin diversity bias, which occurs when certain demographics are underrepresented in the data used to train models. As a result, when these systems interact with society, historically disadvantaged groups may not receive the same level of service as others. To tackle this problem, researchers propose a novel auditing method to detect origin diversity bias in video search outcomes by using virtual agents that mimic human behavior. By creating digital personas with real video search queries, investigators can determine if video hosting platforms show a bias towards a particular origin. We demonstrate this method by auditing the bias in YouTube and Vimeo's video search outcomes, revealing a significant underrepresentation of historically disadvantaged groups in YouTube's search results, whereas Vimeo's search outcomes display no bias.

The Wess-Zumino model, a supersymmetric gauge theory, is used as a test case to explore how to combine "monodromy" and "bootstrap" methods for deriving field equation correlations in the loop level. A new technique is developed to sequentially derive forward and backward dispersion relations for these correlations, without relying on assumptions about the theory's analytic properties. A key innovation in this approach is the introduction of "off-shell monodromy operators" used to extend monodromy operators to apply to individual fields, rather than field correlations as a whole. By sequentially applying these relations, we can obtain "omitted component" relations, providing insight into previously underdetermined components of correlation functions. As a first application, we derive a forward dispersion relation for the Wess-Zumino model's key correlation function, specifically for its "omitted component."

We have found 17 elliptic curves, defined over cubic cyclic fields, with 14 $T_{\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3})$-independent points of rank 13. These curves are defined over subfields of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$ and are paired such that each pair has a point of rank 14. Additionally, we have computed the rank of 304 elliptic curves over these cubic cyclic fields with 14 $T_{\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)}$-dependent points, an analysis that also applies to 2280 curves over subfields of $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$.

This research focuses on minimizing energy consumption and meeting throughput requirements in wireless networks affected by interference. By leveraging the properties of interference correlation, a stochastic medium access control (MAC) approach is developed to ensure a guaranteed minimum network throughput while minimizing energy consumption. The proposed MAC strategy involves an adaptive transmission control that responds to changes in network traffic and interference patterns. The algorithm can be efficiently computed using standard optimization tools, and simulations demonstrate that the proposed approach results in significant energy savings and meets high network throughput demands.

Despite the remarkable performance of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), they often struggle with label scarcity, a common issue in real-world settings. Pseudo-labeling, a popular semi-supervised method for generating high-quality labels, is hampered by a key problem: it can't effectively identify unconfident predictions. To overcome this limitation, we've developed Pseudo-Label Enhancement (PLE), an innovative strategy to bolster pseudo-labeling. Specifically, PLE introduces two techniques: 1) Envelope Pseudo-Labeling (EPL) and 2) Label Enhancement (LE). Both methods aim to enhance pseudo-labeling by targeting less confident predictions, either by widening them to include more neighboring nodes (EPL) or by adjusting their features to match groundtruth labels (LE). We've validated the effectiveness of PLE by applying it to multiple benchmark GNN architectures, resulting in notable label accuracy improvements of up to 12.4% in test accuracy on the CiteSeerNf dataset. Moreover, PLE's enhancements have also translated to efficient runtime performance, with training times comparable to existing pseudo-labeling methods.

Deep learning methods for video processing face limitations due to the constraints of frame alignment, which can hinder performance. Traditional approaches involving full video alignment are excessively time-consuming and unnecessary for tasks like video segmentation, where focus is typically on a single frame at a time. A new method called PatchNet has been developed to overcome these challenges by employing short-range template alignment, where only similar frames to the target are aligned. This is combined with a self-attention module and an error-aware loss function to produce results superior to current methods while achieving significant time savings. For instance, PatchNet performs video segmentation 5.64 times faster than state-of-the-art methods while maintaining 94% of their accuracy.

We examine a system of one-dimensional traffic, specifically the TASEF model, where a fixed number of particles of a specific type move through a fixed number of sections, each with a specific capacity, and we develop a method for determining how these particles are distributed across the segments as time progresses. Given a particular distribution at a specific time, we create a formula for determining the probability distribution of particle counts in each segment at subsequent times. This formula allows us to calculate the long-term probability distribution of particle counts in each segment as a ratio of convergent series. By applying a version of the AGEP method, we find that this long-term distribution is a multi-equal-weighted sum of finite convolution-limited series, where each series is a product of powers of the transfer matrix's eigenvalues and a factorial-driven polynomial. We discover that the base of the exponential part of each series corresponds to a root of the generating function for the transfer matrix's eigenvalues, and each series is driven by a specific pattern of particle movement in the system, and we find that the coefficients of the factorial-driven polynomial are related to the signs of the periods in the system's history.

This study investigates how energy harvesting and data transmission coexist in multi-service wireless communication systems, considering power management as a resource allocation issue. To address this, we've developed a novel power management strategy, where a power-splitting ratio for each user is determined through an optimization process. This involves formulating a multi-objective optimization problem to balance energy harvesting and data transmission demands. Due to the non-convex nature of this problem, we've divided it into two separate optimization problems to simplify this complex task. The resulting power-splitting ratios allow for simultaneous energy harvesting and data transmission, where each user allocates a portion of their time for energy harvesting and the remaining for data transmission. To maintain equal user access, we've implemented a fair-blessing policy, where each user is given a chance to harvest energy based on their need. The proposed power management strategy outperforms traditional baseline systems in both energy efficiency and data rate performance.

Superfluid SU(N) Fermi gases with repulsive interactions exhibit an extensive range of multicomponent systems, encompassing polyatomic fluids created using laser-cooled atoms of N=2 (e.g., $^{6}$Li), as well as those with N>2 (e.g., $^{7}$Li-$^{39}$K mixtures) and infinitely complex mixtures of atoms and molecules (e.g., Erbium species). We have developed extensive theoretical frameworks for the latter two types of systems, applying them to fluids with 3 components, developing unique analytical methods and performing intensive numerical analyses to establish comprehensive theoretical frameworks. These frameworks address both single-particle properties and collective behaviors, offering detailed predictions for properties like energy spectra, density matrices, and oscillation modes. These theoreical frameworks can be utilized to determine the most critical characteristics of these complex Fermi gases.

We present a detailed analysis of a standard microwave optomechanical setup using a traditional electrical circuit model. By applying dimensional analysis, we demonstrate that the motion of the mechanical oscillator can be effectively represented as a variable resistance changing the optical cavity's coupling to the driving field. This model is further validated by mapping the system's entire frequency spectrum using network analysis, showing that the system's behavior transitions from the single-pole optomechanical cavity model to the four-pole classical three-matrix model as the mechanical oscillator's damping increases.

We establish a general framework for airiness in a specific context of random matrix theory involving Hermitian quadratic systems. Our analysis reveals a specific class of airy polynomials that arise in this setting and discusses their key properties. These polynomials exhibit symmetry, can be factorized, and their roots form a lattice structure. Furthermore, we prove that these polynomials converge to a Gaussian distribution as the size of the associated matrices grows infinitely large.

This research explores the challenge of developing robots that can effectively track a moving wall in dynamic environments. Building on prior work in unwinding shifts, which is essential for achieving local convergence along curved surfaces, we delve into the more complex concept of general shifts that enable robots to maintain a consistent distance from walls in non-planar settings. We introduce a new theoretical framework, specifically 'unrival' shifts, which enable robots to maintain a consistent distance from walls even in dynamic environments. This framework provides strong convergence guarantees, making it suitable for practical robot applications. Additionally, we simulate and experimentally validated our findings on a quadcopter robot that successfully tracked a moving ball in various scenarios.

This article further explores and develops the concept of chiral aspects in 2dcft within the pAQFT framework, building upon a previously published study.  It specifically investigates how these aspects relate to a massless scalar field in globally hyperbolic 2-dimensional spacetimes.  The study identifies subalgebras that contain either chiral or anti-chiral observables, constructing these explicitly and showing they are embedded in the full theory's algebra.  It also establishes that the construction of these subalgebras is Cauchy surface-independent and yields a well-defined covariant theory on the space of null geodesics.

Smoke exposure is a significant concern for surgeons' eye health during laparoscopic surgeries. Proper smoke removal through improved camera lenses or image processing techniques could minimize the negative effects of smoke on surgeons' vision. We are investigating whether smoke-reducing images or processing methods can advantageously impact human performance in a smoke-related task. Our research involves two primary approaches: Firstly, we assess whether smoke-filtering lenses or image enhancement techniques can aid human performance in a task related to smoke. Secondly, we explore whether smoke-reducing images or processing methods can benefit a model's accuracy in a smoke-related task. Our study compares the effectiveness of different smoke-reducing lenses, as well as noise injection and convolutional neural network (CNN) image processing, against a baseline using standard laparoscopic lenses. The results show that smoke-reducing lenses or image processing can significantly and advantageously impact human performance in a smoke-related task. Additionally, smoke-reducing methods can positively influence a model's accuracy in a smoke-related task, suggesting that smoke-reducing lenses or image processing can be beneficial in a variety of surgical settings.

A crucial factor limiting the widespread adoption of M{\o}lmer-S{\o}rensen gates driven by microwave fields has been the difficulty in producing a stable frequency for the microwave source. To address this, we have developed a method to create stable gates by averaging the frequency of MS gates driven by ac Stark shifted atomic transitions across multiple modes, eliminating the need for precise matching between the microwave and atomic frequencies. Implementing this technique in an experiment involving $^{171}$Yb atoms, we have successfully created a robust gate algorithm resistant to frequency errors, with an average gate fidelity of 99.97 percent when achieving a 99 percent fidelity level. Additionally, we have achieved an average gate fidelity of 99.95 percent with an average gate duration of 12.8 microseconds for a 99 percent fidelity level.

Researchers at Oxford University have developed a novel method using diamond anvil cells and atomic pair distribution function analysis to determine the atomic density around specific distances in specific ceramic materials. This technique has allowed them to observe the paraelectric structure of barium titanate at room temperature, a discovery that challenges the long-held assumption that this structure is centered around a specific titanium position. Instead, the results indicate that the barium and titanium positions are disordered. Furthermore, the team's findings support the idea that another ceramic material, strontium titanate, exhibits a similar disordered structure. These observations suggest that a particular type of distortion in these ceramic materials may be associated with a phenomenon known as ferroelectricity, and that this distortion could be controlled through the placement of certain elements in the material's crystal lattice.

Recent advancements have led to the development of complex stochastic models that integrate multivariate and functional data, allowing for relationships between individual data points and functional data to be modeled. The functional Gaussian graphical model provides a framework for modeling interactions between functional data, while the multi-task Gaussian graphical model addresses interactions between multivariate data with a common dependence on functional data. We build upon these concepts by introducing a novel model, the functional Gaussian graphical framework, which enables the modeling of interactions between functional data and their relationship with multivariate data. We derive relationships between conditional dependencies in the model and the coefficients of linear combinations of functional data, establishing a connection between our model and the graphically correlated functional random coefficient model. We demonstrate the efficacy of our model through applications to simulated and real-world data.

Compiling quantum circuits efficiently into executable forms is a rapidly evolving field. Current methods, although effective, can be too computationally demanding for larger circuits arising from repeating patterns, due to their linear complexity. This study presents two new algorithms that take advantage of a circuit's repeating structure to reduce the complexity of its compilation. The first algorithm leverages a minimal set of unique gate sequences to eliminate redundancy, resulting in a linear time complexity. The second algorithm applies a similar approach within a circuit's gates to eliminate unnecessary qubit resets, also achieving linear complexity. Both algorithms are accompanied by theoretical justifications and experimental validation.

We examine how various architectures of overparametrized neural networks behave in a convex optimization setting, and find that only the tails of the activation functions contribute to optimal solutions. By applying a precise average-case analysis, we discover that networks with Gaussian features and element-wise ReLU activations yield the strongest performance. This outcome contrasts with suboptimal results obtained from other architectures, such as linear models and neural networks with threshold activations. To achieve our analysis, we derive a sharp estimate for the expected eigenvalues of a random positive definite matrix.

We employ the Fr\"{o}hlich model to study polaron formation within a bilayer semiconductor, where local Coulomb interaction between electrons and holes is strong, and interlayer tunneling plays a crucial role. By combining quantum field theoretical methods and variational approaches, our analysis reveals the emergence of mobile excitons as a polaronic outcome. Our results indicate that when tunneling is prominent, the ground state energy of the bilayer system is dominated by excitonic contributions, and this effect is further amplified at low temperatures due to the formation of two-dimensional Landau gaps.

Designing reliable and robust self-localization systems on radio signals is increasingly important, yet difficulties arise due to the fact that radio navigation relies heavily on external factors such as the environment, number of available antennas, and signal quality. To tackle this issue, we propose an adaptive Proportional Integral Derivative (PID) control method grounded in the study of radio signal strength's relationship with location. The proposed approach begins by developing a non-linear model of signal strength with respect to location, which is challenging to establish directly. Instead, we employ a communication transfer technique to build a reliable model, applicable in various real-world scenarios. The resulting system's dynamic characteristics are then analyzed to establish a relationship between the system's error and its derivative. The adaptive PID controller is then designed to achieve optimal tracking performance, including setting the critical parameter for a well-defined marginal stability boundary. The proposed control system's robustness against sudden changes and disturbances is ensured through a simple loop-back feedback loop. The efficacy of our adaptive PID control method is demonstrated through simulations conducted in actual 2D and 3D environments, which reveal better performance compared to the conventional PID control method.

The standard model of particle physics describes nature's fundamental laws, explaining all known natural phenomena via a precise mathematical framework. However, there's a concern that the model might not be universally applicable, prompting researchers to look for its potential flaws. A key test to address this concern involves examining the polarization of gauge boson joint states, specifically $W$ and $Z$, produced through their joint creation in proton-proton collisions. A notable feature of these collisions, detectable by highly sensitive particle colliders, is a favorable signal-to-background ratio, making it an important area of study. A recent study conducted using a 2015-2018 data set from the Large Hadron Collider, leveraging the ATLAS detector and sophisticated statistical methods, revealed a notable alignment between $W$ and $Z$ boson orientations in nearly all relevant configurations, thus revealing crucial evidence supporting the current model's accuracy and imposing stringent limits on any deviations. These research findings also set precise limits on differences between gauge boson orientations, specifically between $|V_{WZ}|^2$ and $|V_{WZ}'|^2$, ranging from 10$^{-3}$ to 10$^{-2}$. A comprehensive analysis of orientation relationships between $W$ and $Z$ bosons provided further constraints on these relationships, making it an essential research area.

The Cotton tensor is defined as the combination of the Weyl tensor's divergence, diverging in four-dimensional spacetimes, and thus can be regarded as an effective measure of gravity in such spacetimes, much like the Ricci scalar is an effective measure of curvature. This paper demonstrates that by employing Noether theorem for 2-forms in four-dimensional spacetimes, the Cotton tensor can be rigorously derived from a variational problem with a fixed variational symmetry, further establishing that the Cotton tensor's value remains invariant across all general relativity solutions. In addition, the Cotton tensor's value remains invariant across all solutions to the Einstein-Hilbert action, both in vacuum spacetimes and when matter is present.
We establish a geometric duality between orthomodular lattices and planar regions bounded by circles, defining geometric orthomodular lattices in the process.

We introduce the Coq Proof Diagram Visualiser, a tool that visualises proof strategies in Coq as interactive diagrams, enabling users to explore and navigate these strategies graphically. It offers a range of features, including customisable visualisation options, interactive navigation and previewing of diagrams before final rendering. Additionally, proof diagrams can be exported as SVG files. The tool builds on Coq's built-in tactics and user-defined tactics, leveraging metadata to create diagram structures. Users can refine and modify tactics using an interactive command system, which provides insights into the underlying algorithm and metadata manipulation. Furthermore, the tool incorporates an extensive library of pre-defined tactics, facilitating efficient and targeted searches. We illustrate the capabilities of the Coq Proof Diagram Visualiser through two practical examples.

We demonstrate that the fourth moment of Hecke-cusp forms is limited by $C(\gamma) \log(d_S)^{4} + O(\log(d_S)^{3}),$ where $d_S$ is the Serre weight level and $C(\gamma)$ is a constant dependent on Newhouse's conjecture for general $\gamma$. This estimate is in line with previous findings by Iwaniec and Sarnak for the case $ \gamma = 1/4$.

In interior point methods (IPMs), an iterative method is employed to solve linear equations, typically facilitated by an acceleration technique such as the conjugate gradient method. For the acceleration process to be effective, it is crucial to establish a precise stopping criterion. The conventional approach to halt the iteration is to check if the residual reduction rate meets a predetermined requirement or if the residual magnitude falls below a specified threshold. Nonetheless, this methodology poses challenges, particularly in quantum interior point methods, where the predetermined requirement is difficult to meet, and the threshold values are not self-explanatory in terms of the solution quality. Alternatively, researchers have suggested monitoring the norm of the direction multiplier or an indicator related to the primal-dual interior point method, and comparing it to a specified tolerance. Nonetheless, this approach may lead to superfluous iterations if the method takes longer to attain a satisfactory norm, albeit the residual reduction rate might be adequate. To address these concerns, we propose an alternative criterion: monitoring the progress of an indicator related to the primal-dual interior point method, specifically at an early stage or with an approximation, and comparing it to a specified tolerance. This criterion can be set to a value derived from the predicted optimal solution or an easily computable approximation, thereby circumventing potential difficulties. The proposed termination criterion was validated through numerical tests involving standard interior point method problems and compared to existing criteria. Additionally, we investigated how interior point methods perform when employed in conjunction with a flexible quantum accelerator, and we provide recommendations

We have derived the $O(\alpha_s^3)$ polarized Wilson coefficients for different quark flavors, enabling the creation of a novel set of differential parton distribution functions (PDFs) and their corresponding evolution equations. By incorporating the $A_{gq}(N)$ matrix, which governs the fractional contributions of valued quark flavors to the gluon's momentum, we can accurately track and model the gluon's evolution across various scales and kinematics. This work facilitates more precise and nuanced predictions in theoretical physics, particularly in areas like top quark production and precision electroweak measurements. Moreover, the new PDFs' differential nature allows for more detailed and data-driven analyses of parton distribution functions. We have verified the accuracy of the scheme by validating its matching to known PDFs at $O(\alpha_s^2)$ and studying its behavior in various scenarios, including finite-$N$ corrections and uncertainties associated with the scheme's approximation.

Establishing trust in Artificial Intelligence (AI) requires showcasing its benefits and limitations based on real-world case studies. These examples, known as incidents, highlight potential drawbacks and risks associated with relying on AI. Creating a comprehensive database of AI incident cases can facilitate responsible AI development by promoting transparency, education, and safety assessments. This approach is inspired by the aviation industry, which uses incident reports to prevent reoccurrences by leveraging learned best practices. To apply this method in AI, several challenges need to be addressed: defining what constitutes an AI incident, identifying existing cases, and constructing a publicly accessible incident database while maintaining confidentiality when necessary. This paper proposes the creation of an AI Incident Repository (AIR), which includes a framework for documenting incidents and suggests potential applications for teaching responsible AI development.

We've developed a prescription for implementing the renormalization group in numerical simulations using gradient descent techniques. This method incorporates key elements from modern renormalization group theory, such as the concept of a relevant operator and the preservation of physical properties across renormalization steps. We've tested it successfully on a straightforward two-dimensional Ising model, which can however be expanded to tackle more complex problems like quantum systems in three-dimensional spacetime.

Business processes can be represented using two types of specifications: operational details and higher-level definitions. The operational specifications outline the step-by-step process execution, whereas the latter provides a summary of the overall business logic. For a more comprehensive understanding, both aspects need to be considered in modeling, yet current verification methods focus solely on individual specification types. This paper advocates for a combined approach, where both operational and higher-level specifications are taken into account for detecting potential discrepancies. We propose a framework that employs a two-part automata model to represent the specifications and define the concept of adherence based on joint execution paths. Furthermore, we develop a technique to identify and resolve potential discrepancies between the two specification types. This research introduces a novel metric to measure the degree of mismatch between the specifications and presents an algorithm to determine the optimal alignment between the two specification types.

A fundamental challenge in developing quantum software lies in crafting an effective programming language that seamlessly integrates quantum operations with control structures, ensuring precise tracking of computational resources. To address this issue, our previous study introduced a quantum extension to the ML-like functional programming language ML-O, with a focus on sound and efficient reasoning mechanisms. Building upon this work, this paper presents an extension to the type system, incorporating a type of quantum states that aligns with the definitions outlined in [Braun et al., arXiv:2002.03175, 2020]. Furthermore, we introduced a conceptually grounded semantics for proto-Quipper-M, complementing the existing work mentioned above.

In random matrix theory, the behavior of extremes within a matrix is of considerable importance across multiple fields. Although the finite-size scaling of extremes has been extensively studied, there is a lack of comprehensive understanding regarding its scaling limits when approaching criticality. This research aims to address this knowledge gap by investigating the global scaling of extremes in random matrix theory, with a focus on criticality. Through the development of exact extreme statistics for orthogonal and symmetrical matrices approaching criticality, this study reveals new finite-size scaling limits for these cases. Additionally, by relating the derived scaling limits to critical behavior from beyond random matrix theory, this research provides a unified framework for understanding the global scaling of extremes within this theoretical framework.

We introduce a novel approach to quantify the phase of optical signals using ensembles of cold dipoles connected to a high-Q cavity. This method relies on carefully controlled light pulses creating pairs of dipoles in excited states, from which we derive a reliable optical phase detector. By applying the quantum squeezing concept, we show that these ensembles can achieve remarkable sensitivity to optical signals without the need for cooling to the ground state. Furthermore, we highlight the similarities between our detector and advanced optical techniques, and discuss the potential applications of our detection method for entanglement measurements and optical lattice experiments.

A key challenge in constructing a complete genome from fragmented long-read data lies in identifying and extending high-quality continuous sequences, which is referred to as contig production. Due to the extensive size of these sequences, Commerical whole-genome assemblers are incapable of applying on the entirety of the data at once, thus requiring them to break the input into smaller fragments and assemble these individually, subsequently needing to extend or merge the resulting contigs through a secondary analysis. This two-stage approach not only leads to suboptimal results but also results in a significant computational burden. A more direct method involves using a graph construction and in-place assembly approach that can handle sequences of any size within a single unit of work, which has shown promising results but has a major drawback in its memory consumption, specifically its inability to scale without a mainframe class of computers. A new algorithmic approach, however, allows for breaking the input into smaller fragments, and then using a parallel and efficient method to extend and merge these fragments, thus producing complete genome-like contigs, which we call'supercigs'. This approach not only conquers the memory consumption problem by only using a fraction of memory but also provides a notable speedup by leveraging the large amounts of memory available on thousands of compute nodes, which we refer to as distributed-memory parallel new supercig production. In tests using real genomes and artificial data, this new method consistently produces more supercigs and demonstrates a substantial time-to-market advantage over other methods,

A novel logistic equation, incorporating delay, is examined in an abstract mathematical environment to understand its dynamic implications when the inherent rate of increase exceeds one. 

Establishing a boundary layer near the equilibrium point enables transformation into a finite system governing the behavior of solutions, particularly their approaches to the equilibrium point. 

It's discovered that solutions exceeding a certain threshold initially move closer to the equilibrium point, then diverge in opposite directions, with solutions initially below this threshold converging towards the equilibrium point. 

The critical threshold is found to be directly proportional to the delay period and initial conditions, with solutions' long-term trajectories determined by their distance from this threshold, leading them to either approach or recede from the equilibrium point in an oscillating pattern. 

The model's relevance is drawn from population studies, where negative feedback is delayed due to the inherent life cycle process. 

The study presents a theoretical framework for understanding the delayed logistic equation's behavior, offering insights into the dynamic interactions influencing population dynamics.

The statistical depth family is an increasingly popular tool for measuring multivariate location, with applications in predicting distribution functions, testing hypotheses, and constructing confidence sets. We introduce a new depth measure called ILR-depth, which is based on the Isometric Log-Ratio transformation and specifically designed for use with compositional data. This depth measure is well-suited for data that can be represented by positive ratios, making it applicable to a broad range of contexts including geochemical, microbiome, and income data. We outline the key properties of ILR-depth and illustrate its effectiveness through the development of hypothesis tests and the creation of confidence sets for predicting composition distribution functions in a specific scenario.

A particular class of quantum devices, known as Rabi oscillators, have the capacity to reach a stable ground state, known as Rabi ground state, in which continuous wave functions overlap with each other. However, achieving this state in practice is extremely challenging due to the loss of energy associated with coherent radiation. In a study, researchers have proposed an innovative solution to overcome this problem by incorporating a quantum system that undergoes slow changes. Using a combination of ideal and imperfect components, they have demonstrated that in a specifically designed hybrid device consisting of two quantum systems and a waveguide, it is possible to achieve a stable ground state with minimal energy loss. The hybrid device includes an insulating Josephson junction and a circuit that produces resonant energy transmission. Through theoretical analysis, researchers have shown that this device can reach a stable ground state with minimal energy loss and that the device exhibits unique properties in its transition period. The study has confirmed that this hybrid device has the capability to reach a stable ground state with minimal energy loss and that the device exhibits unique properties in its transition period.

The beta-decay properties of neutron-deficient 50Ge isotopes have been studied in-depth using advanced techniques. Specifically, a genetic algorithm was employed to analyze the beta-delayed protons and trions as a combined entity, providing insight into their individual beta-delayed proton spectra. Calculations based on large-scale shell-model simulations revealed that the beta-delayed proton emission from 49Ge to 45Ge can be accurately explained by a 0p structure, with certain proton transitions exhibiting unique patterns. Furthermore, the cumulative proton energy distributions and initial proton energy spectra were found to align closely with the theoretical predictions, thereby validating the simulations. Moreover, these results validated the earlier findings on nuclear level densities and initial proton energy spectra, which were initially based on the beta-delayed protons from 49Ge. Additionally, the study compared the nuclear properties of 50Ge and 50Ge with those of 50Ge, revealing distinct differences between these isotopes and proposing an explanation for these discrepancies through an analysis of the nuclear structure.

A new technique called Bρ-defined isochronous mass spectrometry has been introduced to perform high-precision mass measurements on short-lived nuclei. This method relies on tracking the motion of ions in a constant magnetic field and an alternating electric field to determine the mass-to-charge ratio of the ions. By leveraging a unique beam line at the Lanzhou CSRe, researchers measured the mass of ^{23}Na with precision of 35 times better than the previous best measurements, achieving a precision of 35 eV/(u) or 5.5*10^-10. This level of precision is now accessible to experimentalists due to the enhanced capabilities of the isochronous mass spectrometry system.

The All Nearest Neighbour Optimisation collaboration aims to accelerate the development of hybrid Monte Carlo algorithms used in lattice field theory by providing high-performance, multi-threaded code to the scientific community. For this purpose, we have standardized and optimized the MNIST dataset neural network simulator, a key tool for testing our algorithms, in Fortran 90. This paper outlines the requirements and technical details of our standardization process, before explaining how we have met these requirements through the ANNOVA framework.

This research addresses the task of printed and handwritten text recognition by incorporating a novel approach that favors regular expression patterns in the recognition process. Unlike existing methods, we propose a comprehensive strategy to identify the most relevant regular expressions matching the recognized text features. This is achieved through a dynamic programming table analysis, identifying and prioritizing the preferred patterns. This innovative approach is further optimized by limiting the number of possible regular expression variations. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, yielding a significant improvement of text accuracy by 23.5% and 12.5% overall, respectively.

The production of top and bottom quarks in proton-nucleus collisions at high energies has been examined. A Markov-chain Monte Carlo simulation, called {\tt TROUBADOUR}, was used to model this process. It was discovered that the production of these quarks is affected by color fields in nuclei in a complex manner, particularly visible in the distribution of top quark transverse momentum. Furthermore, {\tt TROUBADOUR} was used to determine that the production of one or more jets, relative to the proton-nucleus baseline, would not exceed 0.5 and 0.7 times that of the proton baseline for 5 and 10 TeV collisions, respectively. Additionally, the examination revealed that the examination of exclusive di-leptons, specifically muon pairs, in these proton-nucleus collisions may provide a valuable means of assessing the color fields in these collisions. It was estimated that the examination of these muon pairs could be observed in a 100 inverse microbarn exposure at the RHIC beam energy, while exceeding 1000 inverse microbarns would be required at the LHC-X2 energy, resulting in a muon pair count of approximately 4600, with both observations providing a 95% confidence level.

This study focuses on key elements of text-to-sQL translation, specifically schema linking, field recognition, and relation identification. We introduce a novel, end-to-end model capable of completing all three tasks simultaneously, augmenting it with two auxiliary tasks to enhance overall performance. Through comprehensive evaluations, we demonstrate that our model surpasses current state-of-the-art benchmarks in zero-shot settings, while also achieving comparable results in few-shot conditions. Notably, our model's integration of auxiliary tasks yields a substantial performance boost of 4.44% and 2.11% in zero-shot and few-shot environments, respectively.

The ongoing LoTSS survey is conducting a thorough observation of the Northern sky to better understand radio sources and improve our knowledge of cosmological phenomena. By analyzing data from the first 0.5 sr of the Northern sky, researchers have made progress in studying the dependence of source count data on frequency and brightness.
